extracted.intended_audience: aspiring freelance producers in TV, film, and live events
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and on-the-job criteria for working as a freelance producer across pre-production, production, and post-production on TV, film, and live events. Covers required skills, day-to-day responsibilities, and professional habits for sustaining a freelance production career.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability to changing projects
rubrics_metrics.description: “Because I am a freelance producer the project or show I am working on is always changing, which to me is the fun part!”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to move between different shows and project phases; enjoy variety. Expect changing responsibilities depending on whether you’re in pre-production, production, or post-production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing pre-production responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: In pre-production you are busy gathering together all the logistics, making sure casting and the hiring of crew is under way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate logistics, oversee casting and crew hiring, and maintain communication with network/studio to ensure everyone is on the same page.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-set production management
rubrics_metrics.description: When a show is in production I am usually on set making sure everything is running smoothly and that we are staying on time and on budget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor schedule and budget during shooting; troubleshoot problems quickly; keep the production running efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-production oversight and closing duties
rubrics_metrics.description: After the production, there is post-production where, if there is any editing, I mark notes on first cuts and give feedback to the editors... If there isn’t any real editing involved I work on closing out the books, finalizing any paperwork, and submitting reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide editorial notes, manage approvals, finalize financials and paperwork, and submit required reports to close the project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to work irregular hours and manage stress
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the cons are that your schedule is not always consistent. Shooting days can go long and there are often a lot of last minute fires to put out and deal with, which can be stressful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared for long days and last-minute crises; develop resilience and stress-management strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constant self-marketing and job-hunting
rubrics_metrics.description: You are always looking for the next job. You are in a continuous state of hustle and job hunting. Networking will be your best friend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively search and pitch for new work between contracts; cultivate relationships that lead to future opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Networking and relationship-building
rubrics_metrics.description: Be nice to everyone... networking is huge... Join as many professional groups as you can and be sincere... I volunteer a lot with the Producer’s Guild of America and it has been a wonderful way to meet other producers and connect on a more personal level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make genuine connections, volunteer in industry organizations (e.g., PGA), and leverage professional groups to expand your network and find jobs or collaborators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational and multi-tasking skills
rubrics_metrics.description: You need to be organized and good at keeping a lot of balls in the air. If you can’t multi-task then you need not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track many simultaneous tasks and deadlines; use project-management practices because you are essentially the project manager making sure the show is a success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budgeting and financial thrift
rubrics_metrics.description: It is also helpful if you are a whiz with budgets and can squeeze every penny where you can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be comfortable creating and managing budgets, finding cost savings, and ensuring productions stay within financial constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership, tone-setting, and crew morale
rubrics_metrics.description: As the producer on set, it is your job to set the tone... keep things positive and get your crew good food. (Lol—but seriously, a happy well fed crew goes a long way.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead by example, maintain positivity, and take actions (like providing good food) that keep morale high and promote smooth collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence and responsibility under pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: You have to have confidence in yourself, your team, and your work—or at least fake it! Others will be looking to you for advice and feeding off of your emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Project confidence, make decisions, and provide steady leadership even when uncertain; prepare to be relied upon during stressful moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpersonal skills and working with diverse personalities
rubrics_metrics.description: You need to be able to work well with a variety of personalities and be a people person. This job is all about the connections and relationships you build.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt communication and management style to different team members and stakeholders; prioritize maintaining good long-term working relationships with investors, crew, and collaborators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivering results: timeliness and budget compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether it’s investors to crew members willing to work with you again. You also need to be able to get things done... can they actually get the work completed in a timely manner, and under budget?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate reliability by completing tasks on schedule and within budget to build reputation and secure repeat collaborators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-care planning for lack of employment benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Because you are freelance and contracted for a certain time period you do not get paid vacations, sick days, insurance, or 401ks. You have to plan your doctor’s appointments and holidays in the gaps when you are not working.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage personal scheduling and finances to compensate for lack of employer benefits; plan medical appointments and time off between gigs.
